Disassembling the Yandex Lavka search service

From Aho–Corasick to a multi-layer ML “burger” on C++ — how a quick-commerce search backend was actually built, and what breaks when you turn each layer off.

Author Nikolai Smirnov · ML Engineer, Yandex Lavka Search
Original habr.com/…/924198
Published 10 July 2025
Reading time ~13 min

Hi! I’m Nikolai Smirnov, an ML engineer on the Yandex Lavka search team. In this article I’ll share a bit of the back story.

How our team built the search service step by step — starting with the Aho–Corasick algorithm, then SaaS solutions, then Market — and ended up with our own architecture in C++ on userver, with a multi-layer “burger” of ML models. Why Lavka’s search needs several technologies at once — BM25, DSSM, BERT, CatBoost — and what each is good for. How our search collects data about you and the products, and why ML models have to be retrained on a schedule.

Together we’ll also “break” production — we’ll see what happens if you switch off one of the models, and why even the most advanced neural networks aren’t a silver bullet. There’ll be a bit of history, the most interesting bits of the architecture, engineering findings, and live examples of how Lavka’s search makes decisions. If you’re curious how search actually works — let’s go.

Chronicles of search finding the right path

A short historical detour. Search in Lavka began with the Aho–Corasick algorithm in 2020. It was modified for product search — matching against name, categories, and synonyms, with the name weighted highest, naturally. It handled some simple typos, but couldn’t, for example, figure out that «вожв» is in fact two typos in the four-letter word «вода» (“water”).

The next stage, in 2021, was a move to SaaS (Search as a Service) — Yandex’s general-purpose internal service for search over arbitrary documents. It didn’t account for Lavka’s specifics, but overall it was decent. We still use it as a baseline when measuring integral improvements in our search-model quality.

Then, also in 2021, the search team partnered with the search-portal team and switched onto the Yandex Market engine. Under it lay an inverted index and a CatBoost ranking model. We built pipelines that fed product data into the search index and wrote a service that proxied search calls into Market’s perimeter.

Market is excellent at finding products, accounting for many factors including CTR and purchase rate. It looked like a perfect fit for Lavka. On top of that, the DevOps and overall engineering culture in the large Market team let us train and embed custom Lavka ML models and roll them out almost independently of other teams; Market’s infrastructure also gave us plenty of headroom for scaling. But ultimately we drifted towards a solution on our own rails — which is what this article is about.

For those interested in the history, here’s a more detailed write-up of the evolution of search in Lavka by Vanya Khodor.

The search service from a bird’s-eye view

At the top level, Lavka’s search service looks like a typical service with machine learning under the hood. It has three important parts:

  1. Runtime, where ML models are applied and users get a relevant search result list.
  2. The system that collects and delivers data for training ML models.
  3. The training pipeline that produces models which then ship into the runtime.

Schematically:

Before diving into the architecture — the way you would in a System Design interview — let’s nail down the important characteristics of the problem:

Q.What’s the daily audience of search in Yandex Lavka? What RPS should we expect?

A.Hundreds of thousands of customers per day, generating around several hundred queries per second at peak.

Q.What user data do we keep?

A.Order history, embeddings, and a few dozen counters such as average basket value. Around 10 KB per user.

Q.How many documents do we search over?

A.~100K products. Product metadata: name, description, composition, price, and a handful of others.

Q.How do we treat out-of-stock items — ignore them, or remove them from results? How many warehouses, and what’s the typical assortment per warehouse?

A.Out-of-stock items are not shown. Around 1K warehouses, each with ~5K items in stock out of an assortment of 20K.

Two more functional requirements worth flagging:

  • Search over partial queries — e.g. “mol” should find “milk”.
  • Search must be personalised — for broad queries like “sour cream”, the top results should be the sour cream you actually buy.

A user query from the front end (Lavka, Eda, Go and Market mobile apps, plus the web client) lands on client-api. This is a coarse-grained service responsible for fetching products from the catalog and from search. It resolves the warehouse the order will be shipped from, and calls the search service, which returns a list of product IDs relevant to the query. Inside search, in order:

  1. Collect user data from kv-user-storage.
  2. Pre-process the query — compute embeddings, normalise text.
  3. Generate candidate items via ML models.
  4. Filter candidates by warehouse availability.
  5. Compute the features needed to run the ranking model.
  6. Apply business rules and produce the final ordered list of product IDs.

The availability filter deserves a separate mention. It sits as close to candidate generation as possible, and here’s why: typically only about ¼ of the full assortment is in stock at a given warehouse, so it would be wasteful to compute heavy ranking-model features for ¾ of the candidates that won’t survive. So search keeps an asynchronously updated cache: per warehouse, we build a Quotient filter (an alternative to a Bloom filter) supporting two operations:

  • add the ID of an item that’s in stock at the warehouse;
  • check whether a given ID is in the filter.

A Quotient filter is a probabilistic structure that guarantees no false negatives. If the item was added to the filter, it’s definitely returned by the check; with some probability (we run at ~0.99) it can return false positives (the item is not actually in stock, but the filter says it is). The result: compact storage of availability info at around 10 KB per warehouse, and a fast predicate.

Once it has the list of products, the orchestrator enriches their IDs with assorted metadata from a cache layered on top of the catalog service to render the product card on the front end — image, name, price, discounts.

That’s the high-level picture. Now let’s look inside the search service’s machinery and see how it serves ML models in production.

A day in the life of an ML service pod

However impressive an ML model’s offline metrics are, the success of its deployment depends heavily on the efficiency of the inference code around it. Let’s see who serves the search service’s ML models and how, by following one day in the life of a search pod:

The search service is written in C++ following a REST style, on top of the open-source userver framework. The diagram shows the burger of ML models — we’ll get to it shortly. The burger needs features at its inputs to make predictions; features are computed at request time from the query text and from data about the products and the user.

Models learn about products from the shard file — a binary file that stores precomputed statistics like a product’s order count, CTR, purchase rate in a given geo, and other useful signals.

The user profile, in the form of counters derived from purchase history, is fetched from a fast key-value store.

The shard with products is updated several times a day: a few new SKUs appear daily, and they need to be searchable as quickly as possible.

On the way out of the ML stage, all features — whether precomputed from counters and shard-file statistics or computed at request time — are written into the features log via a message broker, and from there end up in long-term MapReduce tables (the part later used for training).

Beside the shard-file pipeline there’s a second one: a pipeline of retrained DSSM models. DSSM is used to generate candidates relevant to the query. Fresh models keep search quality from degrading on new entries in Lavka’s assortment, and surface them better in the result list.

The burger also contains ranking and filtering models, deployed into the pod by CI on developer demand — for example before A/B experiments.

Before diving into the search service’s ML models, let’s see where they get their training data.

Training data for the models

When a user in the Lavka app taps on any item in the result list, opens its card, adds it to the cart, or scrolls past in the feed, all those actions are sent as logs into a special storage — User Frontend Logs. They then become available in a prepared DWH table called User Actions. The table has an action_type column, which makes it visible that one item was added to the cart and bought, while another was scrolled past with no interaction.

In parallel, a request goes to the backend, where features are computed for each item and stored in long-term storage as item features. By request ID we can join the two halves and obtain a dataset describing how the user interacted with each item. That’s the training data for a new model.

Skipping ahead: this is how the dataset for the ranking model is built — its target is whether the cart was updated, so the model predicts a ranking score that grows with the probability of purchase. The irrelevant-item filtering model is trained on a different target, but more on that below.

Training itself splits into three parts: assemble the dataset, train the model, then test and validate that what came out is actually good.

Now we can move on to the ML models inside the search service and pin down each one’s role in the fight for results users actually like.

Down the ML rabbit hole

In one of his talks, Valery Babushkin compared ML system design to a rabbit hole — the deeper you go, the more side passages branch off, and you can disappear quite far down any of them. I’ll try not to wander too far from the request-handling pipeline, so we can verify in practice the role each model plays in producing relevant results.

The runtime ML part of the search service is a layered structure shaped like a burger.

The top layer is the models that find items relevant to the query. Below them are the functional layers — filtering and ranking formulas.

We’ll look at how each works, and then we’ll lightly break production with special toggles that disable almost any part of the model burger. To be clear: the toggles are only available from the Lavka search admin panel, not from the front end — so the screenshots below differ from the production UI, but the substance is the same. We’ll check, in practice, what each model contributes to the quality of the result list.

Where search begins

The most important stage in producing the result list is generating the candidate items that answer the user’s query. Here we use DSSM neural networks, BERT distilled into DSSM, and the BM25 algorithm.

CartUpdate DSSM (Deep Structured Semantic Models). A two-tower neural network: one tower produces a query embedding, the other (the document tower) produces a product embedding.

Schematically:

[Query]    -> [ Query Tower    ]      [Document] -> [ Document Tower ]
                       |                                        |
              [Query Embedding]                  [Document Embedding]
                            \                  /
                            [ Compute similarity ]

During training the model receives many pairs — a query and the product the user purchased after it. The query is mapped into an N-dimensional vector (embedding) by the query tower. The same happens to the product — its name, description, brand, and other attributes go through the document tower. We compute cosine similarity between the query and product vectors. The loss optimises both towers’ weights so that relevant pairs are pulled together (high cosine similarity) and irrelevant ones pushed apart.

Product embeddings are computed offline by the trained document tower and stored in an HNSW index, which is loaded into the service pods inside the shard file every few hours. When you search in Lavka, the query tower computes the query embedding, and we run a fast nearest-neighbour search against the HNSW index.

This model performed well on launch compared with full-text search on Market’s inverted index, and for a while it was the main candidate generator in our service. It does have one quirk, though: new SKUs and brands that don’t look like anything in the training set rise poorly as candidates. That’s what pushed the team to build the DSSM retraining pipeline mentioned earlier — every few days the existing DSSM is retrained on the fresh assortment and automatically delivered to the search-service pods.

BERT → DSSM. A BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) model, fine-tuned on Yandex Lavka’s assortment and distilled into DSSM, helps with deep text understanding. It improves embedding quality and helps find products on non-trivial queries whose text doesn’t literally appear in the product’s metadata.

BM25. An algorithm based on tf-idf that scores text relevance from term frequencies in the query and the document. The terms — for instance, character trigrams (“kra-ras-asn-sny-ny”) and word bigrams (“red banana”) — are keys in a precomputed inverted index, and the values are frequency-weighted lists of documents containing the term.

Which candidate model is best?

Before we drop down to the lower layers (filtering and ranking), let’s see what would happen to Lavka’s search if it ran with only one of the candidate generators at a time.

The somewhat tricky query “vegetables for borscht” expects the model to grasp the semantics of the query. Below are top candidates from BM25, CartUpdate DSSM, and BERT DSSM, in each model’s order of decreasing relevance.

BERT DSSM, as the smartest model, looks pretty good: if I were making soup I’d take the first two items. BM25’s output looks strange, doesn’t it — but you now know why. CartUpdate DSSM aced it — almost every result on that list goes straight into the borscht-builder’s cart.

The query “healthy snacks” leaves no chance for BM25 — full-text search just can’t do that — while the neural networks do well, with BERT DSSM subjectively returning the more “healthy” snacks.

It might look like BM25 could simply be replaced by the other two. It can’t. DSSM models have inertia — they need a training stage. Take a product that appeared a couple of days ago, “Watermelon cubes ‘From Lavka’, 500 g”. Both neural networks miss it; BM25 nails it.

Why? BERT DSSM was trained once and the team chose not to set up a retraining pipeline for it for now — the gains weren’t obviously worth the human and compute cost. New SKUs do get embeddings computed by the document tower and end up in the shard file, which lets the model surface them at all, just not necessarily near the top.

Another characteristic example, searching for a new product and brand — “Globus cucumbers”:

BM25 finds exactly the right product in first place. The other two stand aside — precisely because of inertia. Interestingly, CartUpdate DSSM at least returns other pickled cucumbers, while BERT DSSM, which isn’t retrained on the fresh assortment, doesn’t cope at all.

So the models complement one another: when one fails, the others cover.

From the burger’s top layer (candidate generators), we descend to the lower layers — filtering and ranking.

Filtering and ranking the candidates

The candidate items are pooled into a single set; now BERT DSSM, CartUpdate DSSM, and BM25 each score every element of that set so each candidate gets its own grade.

Scoring is much like grading at a thesis defence — each examiner gives the work their own mark. The committee is mixed: academics and people from industry. Academic novelty and presentation are usually best judged by the academics; practical applicability by the practitioners.

In our search, CartUpdate DSSM bakes more knowledge about purchase rate into its embeddings; BERT DSSM bakes in textual semantics; BM25 picks up shared substrings between the query and the product name.

All scores go to the chief judge (continuing the analogy — the committee chair). In our service, the chair is CatBoost — trained on the candidate-generator scores to separate relevant from irrelevant items. We call it the filtering formula. Its training target is the relevance grade of (query, product) pairs on a scale from rel+ to non-rel. A red banana in first place for the query “red ban” is rel+ — the searched item and its attribute both match.

The grading is done by humans and bots, and the bots are catching up to humans on labelling quality. For a search service, the filtering stage cannot be overrated — “stupid” results hit a search’s reputation hardest. Imagine you want to buy a Lego set for your favourite nephew, and instead make a discovery you can never un-see — that Lavka sells beef lung treats for dogs.

That one is, honestly, harmless. Far less pleasant is when queries like “gluten-free”, “halal”, or “lenten” return items that don’t actually have those properties.

We’ll leave this layer un-broken — it’s our active growth area, and users will soon see properly good filtering. The team will write that one up separately, in another article or at a conference.

Back to the last ML stage in search — ranking. The idea is that the items most likely to be purchased land at the top — e.g. the cheese you buy most often shows up near the top of the screen. CatBoost runs here too, only as a ranking model. To make results personalised, training is fed personal user features — precomputed statistics from purchase history. At query time those features are pulled from the kv-user-storage KV store and handed to the model to predict the ranking score.

You can replicate the experiment yourself: search for the same thing in Lavka while logged in, and again in an incognito tab. You’ll see the difference.

Climbing back out of the rabbit hole — takeaways

Quality e-commerce search is not a heap of random models — it’s a thought-through, engineering-heavy ML system in which every layer and component pulls its weight. A couple of takeaways for anyone working on, or building out, search and recommendation systems:

  • Many models is a strength. Neural networks (DSSM, BERT) are great at understanding query meaning and complex user intents, while the more “traditional” BM25 stays indispensable for new SKUs and new brands that the neural nets miss because of rollout and retraining inertia.
  • Reliable pipelines for product data, user events and history, and retrained models are inseparable from search quality. Break a link in the chain and degradation is inevitable.

Search in Yandex Lavka has come a long way — from simple name matching to a complex multi-level ML system in which every part, from candidate generation to ranking, plays an important role in producing a relevant, useful result list for the user.
